lesson.title: Reflexives & Daily Routine
lesson.subtitle: ik was me, ik voel me — Dutch uses a reflexive where English often uses nothing

hook.title: The Verb Comes Back to the Subject
hook.content: Dutch often adds a reflexive pronoun where English says nothing: ik was me, ik voel me goed, wij vergissen ons. The pronoun mirrors the subject.

pattern.title: Me, je, ons, zich
pattern.content: First person me, second je, first plural ons, third person zich. Ik was me, jij wast je, wij wassen ons, hij wast zich. The reflexive is part of the verb's meaning.
pattern.linguist_note: The reflexive set descends from the same pronouns as English myself/yourself; Dutch uses it more often because many verbs are lexically reflexive.
pattern.trap_note: Zich is only third person. Do not say ik was zich; first person is ik was me.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Reflexives & Daily Routine):
exercises.target_answer: wassen, voelen, vergissen, aankleden, scheren, zich
exercises.meaning: to wash, to feel, to be mistaken, to dress, to shave, himself, herself, itself, themselves
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Reflexives & Daily Routine": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik was me.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Reflexives & Daily Routine”.

cues: The pattern: Me, je, ons, zich
exercises.explanation: “Ik voel me goed.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Me, je, ons, zich.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Zich is only third person. Do not say ik was zich; first person is ik was me.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Wij vergissen ons.” is word-for-word “We mistake us.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Me, je, ons, zich.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Zij kleedt zich aan.” reuses only material taught in “Reflexives & Daily Routine” — Me, je, ons, zich.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Zij kleedt zich aan.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Me, je, ons, zich.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “He shaves.”
twist.explanation: Scheren takes zich in the third person; the reflexive is part of the action.

summary.outcome: Use the reflexive set with daily verbs and separable aankleden.
summary.takeaway: A reflexive verb points the action back at its subject.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Reflexive Gym.

wassen.etymology_derivation: English wash and Dutch wassen are the same verb.

voelen.etymology_derivation: English feel and Dutch voelen are the same verb; f voiced to v.

vergissen.etymology_derivation: A prefixed verb; the reflexive me is part of the idiom.

aankleden.etymology_derivation: Separable: aan + kleden ('clothe'), with a reflexive pronoun.

scheren.etymology_derivation: English shear is the same verb; Dutch also uses it for shaving.

zich.etymology_derivation: The third-person reflexive, covering all third-person subjects.
